a: Slipping a fake instruction card into a restaurant's menu so every diner who reads it follows your orders.
e: XSS runs in the victim's browser; SQLi runs against the server's database.

a: Writing 'and also open the safe' on a bank withdrawal slip, and the teller just does it.
e: Parameterized queries stop SQLi at the source; a WAF only adds a filter layer.

a: A public wanted-poster ID number, so everyone talks about the same vulnerability by the same name.
e: A CVE names a vulnerability; CVSS tells you how severe it is.

a: A hurricane scale for vulnerabilities — a single number from 0 to 10 that says how bad the storm is.
e: CVSS rates technical severity; real priority also depends on your environment.

a: The puppeteer's strings: infected machines quietly phone home to receive their next orders.
e: Blocking or detecting C2 beacons cuts attackers off from compromised hosts.

a: Muddy footprints and a broken window latch — clues proving someone already got in.
e: IoCs are reactive artifacts like hashes and IPs; TTPs describe attacker behavior.

a: A trojan horse with a remote-controlled puppet inside, letting the attacker drive your PC from afar.
e: A RAT disguises itself as legitimate software, then hands full control to its operator.

a: A burglar's signature style — how they case houses, pick locks, and escape — rather than one fingerprint.
e: TTPs, mapped in MITRE ATT&CK, are harder for attackers to change than IoCs.

a: The extra toolbars that sneak in when you click 'Next, Next, Finish' too quickly.
e: PUPs install with technical consent, so they're unwanted rather than strictly malicious.

a: The emergency exit plan of a Windows program — attackers rewrite the map so the exit leads to their code.
e: SEH overwrites hijack the exception handler; SafeSEH and SEHOP mitigate them.

a: A vault needing a key, a code, and your fingerprint — stealing one isn't enough.
e: MFA needs different factor types; two passwords are still single-factor.

a: A wristband at a festival: show ID once at the gate, then walk into every stage.
e: SSO is convenient but makes one login a high-value target; pair it with MFA.

a: A signed letter of introduction from your employer that a partner company accepts at its door.
e: SAML passes signed XML assertions, typical for enterprise web SSO.

a: Handing a valet key to the parking attendant — it drives the car but can't open the trunk.
e: OAuth grants scoped access to resources; it is authorization, not authentication.

a: The valet key from OAuth plus a name badge proving who is holding it.
e: OIDC adds an ID token so OAuth can also authenticate the user.

a: Asking the company switchboard operator to look up anyone's office, phone and team.
e: LDAP on 389 is cleartext; LDAPS on 636 adds TLS.

a: A central security desk that every Wi-Fi access point and VPN calls to check IDs.
e: RADIUS uses UDP and encrypts only the password; TACACS+ encrypts everything.
m: Remote Authentication Desk In Use Somewhere

a: Keycards issued by job title: every nurse gets the nurse card, every doctor the doctor card.
e: RBAC ties permissions to roles, not people, which simplifies onboarding and audits.

a: The HR and security office deciding who you are, what badge you get, and when it's revoked.
e: IAM covers all identities; PAM focuses only on high-privilege accounts.

a: Checking out the master key from a guarded cabinet, on camera, for a limited time.
e: PAM vaults, rotates and records admin credentials instead of leaving them standing.

a: A secret handshake that changes every 30 seconds, known only to your phone and the server.
e: TOTP codes come from a shared seed plus the current time, so clocks must agree.

a: The network gear's private security desk, checking ID, permissions and logs in three separate steps.
e: TACACS+ uses TCP 49, encrypts the full payload, and separates all three A's.
m: Terminal Admins Can Authenticate Commands Securely

a: The ticket office at a theme park: prove who you are once, then collect tickets for each ride.
e: The KDC contains both the AS and TGS, usually on a domain controller.

a: A theme park wristband system: verify at the gate once, then trade the wristband for ride tickets.
e: Kerberos never sends passwords over the network and rejects tickets with excessive clock skew.
m: Keys expire rapidly, but every request obtains service

a: The same Cisco security desk as TACACS+, the version the exam really means today.
e: Modern TACACS+ encrypts the whole payload, unlike RADIUS which hides only the password.
m: Total Admin Command Access Control Security

a: The theme-park wristband: it doesn't open rides itself, but it lets you collect ride tickets.
e: A stolen TGT enables pass-the-ticket attacks, so its lifetime is kept short.

a: The ride-ticket booth where you show your wristband to get a ticket for one specific ride.
e: The TGS exchanges a TGT for a service ticket; the AS issues the TGT.

a: The park entrance gate that checks your ID and puts on your wristband.
e: The AS verifies the user once; later requests go to the TGS.

a: A single ride ticket that only works on the one attraction printed on it.
e: A service ticket is accepted by one service, encrypted with that service's key.

a: Two people proving they know the same password without ever saying it aloud, so eavesdroppers learn nothing.
e: SAE (Dragonfly) resists offline dictionary attacks that break WPA2-PSK.

a: A door that opens only if your department, clearance, location and the time of day all match the policy.
e: ABAC evaluates many attributes per request, far more granular than roles alone.

a: Windows tapping your shoulder: 'Are you sure you want to use admin powers for this?'
e: UAC runs users with standard rights and asks before elevating any action.

a: A sign on the door saying 'closed after 6 PM' that applies to everyone, whoever they are.
e: RuBAC applies the same rules to everyone, such as firewall ACLs or time windows.

a: A nightclub: check your ID, decide which rooms you can enter, and log what you ordered.
e: AAA is the framework; RADIUS and TACACS+ are protocols that carry it out.

a: A doorman's clipboard checked top to bottom — the first matching line decides who gets in.
e: ACLs are processed in order with an implicit deny at the end.

a: A fingerprint door so fussy it keeps locking out the very employees it should admit.
e: FRR is an inconvenience error; FAR is the security error of admitting impostors.

a: A border guard who not only checks passports but opens luggage and knows which app you're carrying.
e: An NGFW identifies applications and users, not just ports, using deep packet inspection.

a: A customs officer who opens every parcel and reads the contents, not just the shipping label.
e: DPI reads payloads, but encrypted traffic must be decrypted first to inspect it.

a: The lobby of a secured building: visitors can reach reception, but not the offices upstairs.
e: Public-facing servers live in the DMZ so a breach doesn't reach the internal LAN.

a: Security at the exit scanning everyone's bags for documents they shouldn't be carrying out.
e: DLP classifies and blocks sensitive data in motion, at rest, and in use.

a: A health screening at the door: no badge, missing patches, or no antivirus means no entry.
e: NAC checks device identity and health before granting any network access.

a: A building where every single door checks your badge, even after you're already inside.
e: ZTNA grants access per application, replacing a VPN's broad network-level trust.

a: A remote control for the company's phones: push settings, enforce PINs, wipe a lost device.
e: MDM enforces policy on devices, including remote wipe if one is lost.

a: Mission control for a power grid, watching and steering equipment spread across hundreds of miles.
e: SCADA supervises widely spread assets, often over legacy and insecure protocols.

a: The nervous system of factories and utilities, where a hack can move physical machinery.
e: In ICS, availability and safety come first, so patching is slow and careful.

a: A rugged little brain bolted to a machine, running its on-off logic all day in the factory heat.
e: PLCs directly drive machinery; Stuxnet showed what happens when they are reprogrammed.

a: A remote weather station reporting gauge readings back to mission control.
e: RTUs sit at remote sites and relay telemetry over long distances.

a: A name tag that announces itself to any reader nearby, whether you meant it to or not.
e: RFID badges can be skimmed and cloned at a distance; shielded sleeves help.

a: A Swiss Army knife appliance: firewall, IPS, antivirus and filtering in one box.
e: A UTM simplifies small networks but creates a single point of failure.

a: A battery bridge that keeps the lights on long enough for the generator to start.
e: A UPS covers minutes of outage; generators handle longer ones.
